claim: The barn owl's midbrain features a map of auditory space where neurons compute horizontal sound location from the interaural time difference (ITD).
source: The barn owl's midbrain features a map of auditory space where neurons compute horizontal sound location from the interaural time difference (ITD).
evidence: This is established knowledge about barn owl auditory neuroscience, supported by the citation context of the manuscript.

claim: Frequency tuning of midbrain map neurons correlates with the most reliable frequencies for the neurons' preferred ITD.
source: Frequency tuning of midbrain map neurons correlates with the most reliable frequencies for the neurons' preferred ITD (Cazettes et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cazettes et al., 2014.

claim: Removal of the facial ruff led to a specific decrease in the reliability of high frequencies from frontal space.
source: Removal of the facial ruff led to a specific decrease in the reliability of high frequencies from frontal space.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by HRTF analysis data presented in Figure 1.

claim: In ruff-removed adult owls, frontally tuned neurons were tuned to frequencies lower than in normal adult owls.
source: In both groups, frontally tuned neurons were tuned to frequencies lower than in normal adult owls, consistent with the change in ITD reliability.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by electrophysiological recordings presented in Figures 3 and 8.

claim: In juvenile owls, frontally tuned neurons were tuned to frequencies lower than in normal adult owls.
source: In both groups, frontally tuned neurons were tuned to frequencies lower than in normal adult owls, consistent with the change in ITD reliability.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by electrophysiological recordings presented in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Juvenile owls exhibited more heterogeneous frequency tuning than adult owls.
source: In addition, juvenile owls exhibited more heterogeneous frequency tuning, suggesting normal developmental processes refine tuning to match ITD reliability.
evidence: This is supported by data showing wider and more variable frequency tuning ranges in juvenile owls presented in Figure 8.

claim: Long-term statistics of spatial cues causally drive the development of midbrain frequency tuning properties.
source: These results indicate causality of long-term statistics of spatial cues in the development of midbrain frequency tuning properties, implementing probabilistic coding for sound localization.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from the experimental manipulations and developmental observations.

claim: Barn owls use interaural time difference (ITD) to compute sound location in azimuth.
source: Barn owls use interaural time difference (ITD), the delay for a sound to reach one ear before the other, and interaural level difference (ILD), the difference in sound intensity between the two ears, to, respectively, compute sound location in azimuth and elevation (Moiseff and Konishi, 1981; Moiseff, 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Moiseff and Konishi, 1981 and Moiseff, 1989.

claim: Barn owls use interaural level difference (ILD) to compute sound location in elevation.
source: Barn owls use interaural time difference (ITD), the delay for a sound to reach one ear before the other, and interaural level difference (ILD), the difference in sound intensity between the two ears, to, respectively, compute sound location in azimuth and elevation (Moiseff and Konishi, 1981; Moiseff, 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Moiseff and Konishi, 1981 and Moiseff, 1989.

claim: ITD and ILD are represented in the barn owl's external nucleus of the inferior colliculus (ICx), creating a topographic midbrain map of sound location.
source: ITD and ILD are represented in the barn owl's external nucleus of the inferior colliculus (ICx), creating a topographic midbrain map of sound location (Knudsen and Konishi, 1978).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Knudsen and Konishi, 1978.

claim: The barn owl shows specialization in its ability to compute ITD from frequencies as high as 10 kHz.
source: The barn owl shows specialization in its ability to compute ITD from frequencies as high as 10 kHz (Wagner et al., 1987; Carr and Konishi, 1990; Köppl, 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Wagner et al., 1987; Carr and Konishi, 1990; and Köppl, 1997.

claim: For sounds originating from frontal locations, ITD cues derived from higher frequencies are less susceptible to corruption from concurrent sounds.
source: HRTF-based analysis has indicated that for sounds originating from frontal locations, ITD cues derived from the higher frequencies of the barn owl's hearing range are less susceptible to corruption from concurrent sounds; while for sounds from peripheral space, ITD cues derived from low frequencies are less susceptible to corruption (Cazettes et al., 2014; Fischer and Peña, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cazettes et al., 2014 and Fischer and Peña, 2017.

claim: For sounds from peripheral space, ITD cues derived from low frequencies are less susceptible to corruption from concurrent sounds.
source: HRTF-based analysis has indicated that for sounds originating from frontal locations, ITD cues derived from the higher frequencies of the barn owl's hearing range are less susceptible to corruption from concurrent sounds; while for sounds from peripheral space, ITD cues derived from low frequencies are less susceptible to corruption (Cazettes et al., 2014; Fischer and Peña, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cazettes et al., 2014 and Fischer and Peña, 2017.

claim: The facial ruff acts as an external ear, modulating the gain and phase of sounds reaching the eardrums.
source: In the barn owl, the facial ruff, a disc of stiff feathers that surrounds the head, acts as an external ear, modulating the gain and phase of sounds reaching the eardrums (Coles and Guppy, 1988; Keller et al., 1998; von Campenhausen and Wagner, 2006; Hausmann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Coles and Guppy, 1988; Keller et al., 1998; von Campenhausen and Wagner, 2006; and Hausmann et al., 2009.

claim: After facial ruff removal, there was a sharp decrease in the reliability of high frequencies coming from frontal locations.
source: After ruff removal, there was a sharp decrease in the reliability of high frequencies coming from frontal locations, with minimal changes elsewhere (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by HRTF-based analysis data presented in Figure 1b.

claim: After ruff removal, changes in reliability were stronger for frequencies above 4 kHz coming from within ±40° of azimuth location.
source: Computing the difference in reliability between the two conditions highlights that after ruff removal, the changes in reliability were stronger for frequencies above 4 kHz coming from within ±40° of azimuth location (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by the difference analysis presented in Figure 1c.

claim: 117 ICx neurons were recorded across two ruff-removed owls.
source: We recorded 117 ICx neurons across the two owls.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental data collected.

claim: The recorded population of ICx neurons in ruff-removed owls spanned ITD tunings of 0–230 µs, which equates to a range of 0–75° azimuth.
source: The recorded population spanned ITD tunings of 0–230 µs, which equates to a range of 0–75° azimuth.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental data collected.

claim: On a population-wide scale, ILD tuning was correlated with ITD tuning in ruff-removed owls.
source: However, on a population-wide scale, ILD tuning was correlated with ITD tuning in these owls (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis presented in Figure 2d.

claim: In normal adult owls, neurons tuned to ITDs near 0 µs are driven by high frequencies.
source: In normal adult owls, neurons tuned to ITDs near 0 µs, or frontal locations, are driven by high frequencies, while neurons tuned to large ITDs, or peripheral locations, are driven by low frequencies (Cazettes et al., 2014), exposing a significant correlation between ITD and frequency tuning (r2 = 0.75, p=5.6e-55).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cazettes et al., 2014 and the correlation analysis.

claim: In normal adult owls, neurons tuned to large ITDs are driven by low frequencies.
source: In normal adult owls, neurons tuned to ITDs near 0 µs, or frontal locations, are driven by high frequencies, while neurons tuned to large ITDs, or peripheral locations, are driven by low frequencies (Cazettes et al., 2014), exposing a significant correlation between ITD and frequency tuning (r2 = 0.75, p=5.6e-55).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cazettes et al., 2014 and the correlation analysis.

claim: In ruff-removed owls, there was a shallower slope of the linear correlation between ITD and frequency tuning (r2 = 0.18, p=1.6e-06) compared to normal owls.
source: In the ruff-removed owls, there was a shallower slope of the linear correlation between ITD and frequency tuning (r2 = 0.18, p=1.6e-06, Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis presented in Figure 3.

claim: The correlations between ITD and frequency tuning in normal and ruff-removed owls were significantly different (t-test: t = 8.97, p=3.0e-19).
source: These two correlations were significantly different (t-test: t = 8.97, p=3.0e-19).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of the two correlation slopes.

claim: The y-intercepts of the regression lines for normal owls (5.6 kHz) and ruff-removed owls (4.6 kHz) were significantly different (t = 7.56, p=4.0e-14).
source: The y-intercepts of the regression lines, which can be used to compare the frequency tuning of frontal neurons, were also significantly different (normal owls = 5.6 kHz, ruff-removed owls = 4.6 kHz; t = 7.56, p=4.0e-14).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of the y-intercepts of the regression lines.

claim: A Mann–Whitney U-test comparing the best frequency tuning of frontally tuned neurons (ITDs ≤ 30 µs) showed significant differences between normal and ruff-removed owls (u = 63, p=7.3e-08).
source: In addition, a Mann–Whitney U-test comparing the best frequency tuning of the frontally tuned neurons, defined here as preferring ITDs ≤ 30 µs (~10° eccentricity), produced consistent results (u = 63, p=7.3e-08).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of frequency tuning between groups.

claim: Frontally tuned neurons of ruff-removed owls showed little responsivity to tones above 6 kHz.
source: In line with this, the frontally tuned neurons of ruff-removed owls showed little responsivity to tones above 6 kHz (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the frequency tuning curves presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: ICx neurons of ruff-removed owls showed little ITD selectivity to frequencies outside their frequency range.
source: ICx neurons of ruff-removed owls showed little ITD selectivity to frequencies outside their frequency range (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), suggesting that these neurons cannot use high frequencies for sound localization.
evidence: This is supported by the ITD tuning curves for different frequencies presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: 43 ICCls neurons were recorded from the two ruff-removed owls in adulthood.
source: We recorded 43 ICCls neurons from the same two ruff-removed owls in adulthood and found the normal frequency tuning range (1–8 kHz) across ITD-selective neurons (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental data collected.

claim: ICCls neurons in ruff-removed owls showed the normal frequency tuning range (1–8 kHz) across ITD-selective neurons.
source: We recorded 43 ICCls neurons from the same two ruff-removed owls in adulthood and found the normal frequency tuning range (1–8 kHz) across ITD-selective neurons (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: ICCls neurons tuned to high frequencies and frontal ITDs were observed in ruff-removed owls.
source: In particular, ICCls neurons tuned to high frequencies and frontal ITDs in ruff-removed owls were observed (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The auditory system in ruff-removed owls is still able to use high frequencies to compute ITDs, but this is not passed onto the ICx.
source: This suggests that the auditory system is still able to use high frequencies to compute ITDs, but this is not passed onto the ICx.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ICCls neurons maintain high-frequency ITD tuning while ICx neurons do not.

claim: In the normal condition, gain was strongest for high frequencies in frontal space, with negative gain at all other locations and frequencies.
source: In line with previous reports (Keller et al., 1998; Cazettes et al., 2014), gain in the normal condition was strongest for high frequencies in frontal space, with negative gain at all other locations and frequencies (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by the gain analysis presented in Figure 5a and citations to previous work.

claim: In the ruff-removed condition, gain remained strongest for high frequencies in frontal space, but expanded slightly to include stronger gain in more peripheral locations.
source: In the ruff-removed condition, gain remained strongest for high frequencies in frontal space, but expanded slightly to include stronger gain in more peripheral locations (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by the gain analysis presented in Figure 5b.

claim: The gain of lower frequencies had a more limited increase to approximately 0 dB after ruff removal.
source: In contrast, the gain of lower frequencies had a more limited increase, to approximately 0 dB (i.e. no net gain change), likely because the facial ruff normally attenuates these sounds (Figure 5a, Coles and Guppy, 1988; Keller et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by the gain analysis presented in Figure 5 and citations to previous work.

claim: High frequencies remain the most audible in frontal locations after facial ruff removal.
source: This analysis suggests that the limited changes in gain across frequencies are insufficient to explain the changes in frequency tuning as high frequencies remain the most audible in frontal locations after facial ruff removal.
evidence: This is inferred from the gain analysis presented in Figure 5.

claim: Recordings were performed from two juvenile owls at 42 and 44 d post hatching.
source: Recordings were performed from two juvenile owls at 42 and 44 d post hatching.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental procedure.

claim: At 42 and 44 d post hatching, the ruff feathers were still within the sheathed stalks.
source: These time points corresponded to ongoing ruff development as the ruff feathers were still within the sheathed stalks, with the ruff not fully developing until approximately 60 d post hatching (Haresign and Moiseff, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by observation and citation to Haresign and Moiseff, 1988.

claim: The ruff does not fully develop until approximately 60 d post hatching.
source: These time points corresponded to ongoing ruff development as the ruff feathers were still within the sheathed stalks, with the ruff not fully developing until approximately 60 d post hatching (Haresign and Moiseff, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Haresign and Moiseff, 1988.

claim: These recordings are the earliest performed during the development of the barn owl's midbrain.
source: To our knowledge, these recordings are the earliest performed during the development of the barn owl's midbrain.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the recordings based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: 39 ICx neurons were identified in juvenile owls.
source: We were able to identify 39 ICx neurons, which showed typical topographic ITD tuning, as well as latencies and thresholds.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental data collected.

claim: ICx neurons in juvenile owls showed typical topographic ITD tuning, as well as latencies and thresholds.
source: We were able to identify 39 ICx neurons, which showed typical topographic ITD tuning, as well as latencies and thresholds.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental observations.

claim: ILD tuning did not change with depth along the dorsal-ventral axis in juvenile owls, as observed in normal adult ICx.
source: However, we found that ILD tuning did not change with depth along the dorsal-ventral axis, as observed in normal adult ICx (Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Mogdans and Knudsen, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and citation to Mogdans and Knudsen, 1993.

claim: There was no correlation between ITD and best frequency in juvenile owls (r2 = 0.18, p=0.28).
source: There was no correlation between ITD and best frequency in the juvenile owls (r2 = 0.18, p=0.28), although this may be attributed to the lack of recorded neurons tuned to ITDs >120 µs (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis presented in Figure 7.

claim: There was a significant difference in best frequency tuning of frontal neurons between juvenile owls and normal adult owls (u = 558, p=5.9e-04).
source: When we compared the best frequency tuning of frontal neurons, there was a significant difference between the juvenile owls and both the normal (u = 558, p=5.9e-04) and ruff-removed (u = 281, p=3.2e-03) adult owls (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is supported by the Mann-Whitney U-test results presented in Figure 8a.

claim: There was a significant difference in best frequency tuning of frontal neurons between juvenile owls and ruff-removed adult owls (u = 281, p=3.2e-03).
source: When we compared the best frequency tuning of frontal neurons, there was a significant difference between the juvenile owls and both the normal (u = 558, p=5.9e-04) and ruff-removed (u = 281, p=3.2e-03) adult owls (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is supported by the Mann-Whitney U-test results presented in Figure 8a.

claim: The mean best frequency of frontal neurons in juvenile owls was 4.9 kHz.
source: The mean best frequency of the frontal neurons in juvenile owls was 4.9 kHz, which is between that of normal and ruff-removed adult owls.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the calculated mean from the experimental data.

claim: There was a significant difference in the high-frequency bounds between juvenile and ruff-removed owls (u = 206, p=6.2e-05).
source: While there was a significant difference in the neurons' high-frequency bounds between the juvenile and ruff-removed owls (u = 206, p=6.2e-05), there was no significant difference between the juvenile and normal adult owls (u = 409, p=0.4).
evidence: This is supported by the Mann-Whitney U-test results.

claim: There was no significant difference in the high-frequency bounds between juvenile and normal adult owls (u = 409, p=0.4).
source: While there was a significant difference in the neurons' high-frequency bounds between the juvenile and ruff-removed owls (u = 206, p=6.2e-05), there was no significant difference between the juvenile and normal adult owls (u = 409, p=0.4).
evidence: This is supported by the Mann-Whitney U-test results.

claim: There was a significant difference in the low-frequency bounds between juvenile and normal adult owls (u = 600, p=3e-05).
source: In contrast, we saw the opposite for the low-frequency bounds: there was a difference between the juvenile and normal adult owls (u = 600, p=3e-05), but no significant difference between the juvenile and ruff-removed owls (u = 466, p=0.7).
evidence: This is supported by the Mann-Whitney U-test results.

claim: There was no significant difference in the low-frequency bounds between juvenile and ruff-removed owls (u = 466, p=0.7).
source: In contrast, we saw the opposite for the low-frequency bounds: there was a difference between the juvenile and normal adult owls (u = 600, p=3e-05), but no significant difference between the juvenile and ruff-removed owls (u = 466, p=0.7).
evidence: This is supported by the Mann-Whitney U-test results.

claim: Juvenile owls' ICx neurons are broader and more heterogeneously tuned to frequency than normal or ruff-removed adult owls.
source: These results are summarized in Figure 8b and suggest that the juvenile owls' ICx neurons are broader and more heterogeneously tuned to frequency than normal or ruff-removed adult owls, which then gets refined during development.
evidence: This is inferred from the frequency bound analysis presented in Figure 8b.

claim: There were significant differences in the responsive frequency range of ICx neurons between juvenile owls and normal adult owls (u = 190, p=0.003).
source: In accordance with this, we found significant differences in the responsive frequency range of ICx neurons between the juvenile owls and both the normal adult owls (u = 190, p=0.003) and ruff-removed adults (u = 221, p=1.6e-04), but not between the normal and ruff-removed adults (u = 418, p=0.73) (Figure 8c).
evidence: This is supported by the Mann-Whitney U-test results presented in Figure 8c.

claim: There were significant differences in the responsive frequency range of ICx neurons between juvenile owls and ruff-removed adults (u = 221, p=1.6e-04).
source: In accordance with this, we found significant differences in the responsive frequency range of ICx neurons between the juvenile owls and both the normal adult owls (u = 190, p=0.003) and ruff-removed adults (u = 221, p=1.6e-04), but not between the normal and ruff-removed adults (u = 418, p=0.73) (Figure 8c).
evidence: This is supported by the Mann-Whitney U-test results presented in Figure 8c.

claim: There was no significant difference in the responsive frequency range between normal and ruff-removed adults (u = 418, p=0.73).
source: In accordance with this, we found significant differences in the responsive frequency range of ICx neurons between the juvenile owls and both the normal adult owls (u = 190, p=0.003) and ruff-removed adults (u = 221, p=1.6e-04), but not between the normal and ruff-removed adults (u = 418, p=0.73) (Figure 8c).
evidence: This is supported by the Mann-Whitney U-test results presented in Figure 8c.

claim: ITD tuning width of frontal neurons was significantly broader in ruff-removed owls (u = 72, p=1.2e-07) compared to normal owls.
source: Analysis of ITD tuning width of frontal neurons showed significantly broader tuning width in ruff-removed (u = 72, p=1.2e-07) and juvenile owls (u = 188, p=0.0028), consistent with their tuning to lower frequencies and the known relationship between frequency tuning and ITD tuning width of midbrain neurons (Takahashi and Konishi, 1986; Wagner et al., 2007; Figure 8d).
evidence: This is supported by the Mann-Whitney U-test results presented in Figure 8d and citations to previous work.

claim: ITD tuning width of frontal neurons was significantly broader in juvenile owls (u = 188, p=0.0028) compared to normal owls.
source: Analysis of ITD tuning width of frontal neurons showed significantly broader tuning width in ruff-removed (u = 72, p=1.2e-07) and juvenile owls (u = 188, p=0.0028), consistent with their tuning to lower frequencies and the known relationship between frequency tuning and ITD tuning width of midbrain neurons (Takahashi and Konishi, 1986; Wagner et al., 2007; Figure 8d).
evidence: This is supported by the Mann-Whitney U-test results presented in Figure 8d and citations to previous work.

claim: In barn owls that developed without a facial ruff, there is an altered relationship between the tunings to ITD and frequency relative to normal adult barn owls.
source: We report that in barn owls that developed without a facial ruff, there is an altered relationship between the tunings to ITD and frequency relative to previous reports from normal adult barn owls (Knudsen et al., 1984; Cazettes et al., 2014).
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by the experimental data.

claim: Ruff-removed barn owls showed on average a decrease in frequency tuning for frontally tuned ICx neurons, from 6 kHz to 4.5 kHz.
source: These ruff-removed barn owls showed on average a decrease in frequency tuning for frontally tuned ICx neurons, from 6 kHz to 4.5 kHz, with no change in frequency tuning width (Figure 8c).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 8.

claim: There was no change in frequency tuning width in ruff-removed owls compared to normal owls.
source: These ruff-removed barn owls showed on average a decrease in frequency tuning for frontally tuned ICx neurons, from 6 kHz to 4.5 kHz, with no change in frequency tuning width (Figure 8c).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 8c.

claim: Neurons immediately upstream of the ICx maintained the ability to resolve ITD at high frequencies in ruff-removed owls.
source: In support of this, neurons immediately upstream of the ICx maintained the ability to resolve ITD at these high frequencies (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the ICCls recordings presented in Figure 4.

claim: The best frequency tuning for frontally tuned ICx neurons in juvenile owls were lower than in normal adults but higher than in ruff-removed owls.
source: The best frequency tuning we found for frontally tuned ICx neurons in juvenile owls were lower than what has been found in normal adults (Cazettes et al., 2014), but higher than what is found in ruff-removed owls (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 8 and citation to Cazettes et al., 2014.

claim: At the time of recording (42-44 days post hatching), the barn owl's ICx frequency tuning is not yet shaped by ITD reliability.
source: This suggests that at this time point the barn owl's ICx frequency tuning is not yet shaped by ITD reliability, which may change rapidly in response to the facial ruff's development.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that juvenile frequency tuning is intermediate between normal and ruff-removed conditions.

claim: Juvenile ICx neurons had slightly wider and heterogenous frequency tuning widths than either normal adult or ruff-removed adults.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we found that juvenile ICx neurons had slightly wider and heterogenous frequency tuning widths than either the normal adult or ruff-removed adults, covering the ranges of both adult groups, but not a width that would indicate that each of these ICx neurons were sampling the entire frequency range available to the barn owl for ITD detection (0.5–9 kHz).
evidence: This is supported by the frequency range analysis presented in Figure 8.

claim: Juvenile owl's ICx shows high heterogeneity in frequency tuning at the time that the facial ruff would begin to grow in.
source: This suggests high heterogeneity in the juvenile owl's ICx frequency tuning at the time that the facial ruff would begin to grow in.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of wider and more variable frequency tuning in juvenile owls.

claim: As the owl develops, individual neurons may sharpen their frequency tuning to match the pattern of ITD reliability the owl experiences during development.
source: As the owl develops, these individual neurons may sharpen their frequency tuning to match the pattern of ITD reliability the owl experiences during development or the neurons that respond to unreliable frequencies could be pruned during development.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the developmental mechanism.

claim: Neurons that respond to unreliable frequencies could be pruned during development.
source: As the owl develops, these individual neurons may sharpen their frequency tuning to match the pattern of ITD reliability the owl experiences during development or the neurons that respond to unreliable frequencies could be pruned during development.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the developmental mechanism.

claim: A juvenile owl undergoes a process to refine the frequency tuning in the ICx based on the pattern of ITD reliability experienced during early-life development.
source: These results suggest a juvenile owl undergoes a process to refine the frequency tuning in the ICx based on the pattern of ITD reliability that the owl experiences during early-life development.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from the developmental observations.

claim: Along normal development, the frequency tuning of frontally tuned neurons changes in a manner consistent with an increase in high-frequency reliability at frontal locations.
source: Along normal development, the frequency tuning of frontally tuned neurons changes in a manner consistent with an increase in high-frequency reliability at frontal locations, determined by the acoustic properties of the facial ruff.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of juvenile and adult frequency tuning patterns.

claim: The difference in frequency tuning of frontally tuned neurons between normal adults and juveniles (rank-biserial correlation, r = 0.55) is smaller than the difference between normal adult and ruff-removed owls (rank-biserial correlation, r = 0.84).
source: It should be noted that the difference in frequency tuning of frontally tuned neurons between normal adults and juveniles (rank-biserial correlation, r = 0.55) is smaller than the difference between normal adult and ruff-removed owls (rank-biserial correlation, r = 0.84).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of effect sizes.

claim: The ruff-removed owls still underwent a refinement in ICx frequency tuning, but toward lower frequencies compared to normal adults.
source: This suggests that the ruff-removed owls still underwent a refinement in ICx frequency tuning, but toward lower frequencies compared to normal adults.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of effect sizes between juvenile-normal and juvenile-ruff-removed differences.

claim: The timing of ruff development, which completes at approximately 60 d post hatching, aligns with previous reports of a critical period in the barn owl.
source: The timing of ruff development, which completes at approximately 60 d post hatching, aligns with previous reports of a critical period in the barn owl, which can remain open to 200 d post hatching (Knudsen et al., 1984; Brainard and Knudsen, 1993; Brainard and Knudsen, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on critical periods.

claim: The shift in frequency tuning likely occurs over the critical period (60-200 days post hatching).
source: Although not directly tested in this study, it is likely that the shift in frequency tuning occurs over this time period.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the timing of ruff development and known critical periods.

claim: The effect of ruff removal on ITD reliability is unlikely to be due solely to a change in gain of sound level.
source: It is unlikely that the effect of ruff removal on ITD reliability is due solely to a change in gain of sound level as this and previous reports found that ruff removal decreases the gain across frequencies, yet the gain remains higher for higher frequencies around 6–8 kHz (Figure 5, Coles and Guppy, 1988; von Campenhausen and Wagner, 2006), inconsistent with the estimated lower ITD reliability of high-frequency sounds in frontal locations for these owls.
evidence: This is inferred from the gain analysis and comparison with ITD reliability changes.

claim: The rate of change of ITD (µs/deg) is not reported to change significantly across frequencies after ruff removal.
source: Likewise, the rate of change of ITD (µs/deg), another significant statistic determining ITD discriminability (Feddersen et al., 1957; Gelfand, 2016; Pavão et al., 2020), is not reported to change significantly across frequencies after ruff removal (von Campenhausen and Wagner, 2006), reducing the possibility of it being an alternative mechanism driving change of frequency tuning.
evidence: This is supported by citation to von Campenhausen and Wagner, 2006.

claim: Gain alone cannot explain the frequency tuning in the ICx.
source: This is consistent with previous work which reported that gain alone cannot explain the frequency tuning in the ICx (Cazettes et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cazettes et al., 2014.

claim: Testing of spatial tuning changes showed no systematic frequency-dependent effects after ruff removal.
source: Additional testing of whether the observed change in frequency tuning of frontal neurons could be determined by the reported changes in the pattern of ITD and ILD across spatial locations after ruff removal (Knudsen et al., 1984; von Campenhausen and Wagner, 2006) showed no systematic frequency-dependent effects (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by the spatial tuning modeling presented in Figure 6.

claim: After ruff removal, there was an increase in the potential efficacy of high frequencies for frontal space.
source: In fact, after facial ruff removal, we noticed an increase in the potential efficacy of high frequencies for frontal space, likely due to ILD being correlated with azimuth after facial ruff removal (Knudsen et al., 1984; Figure 2d).
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial tuning modeling and ILD-azimuth correlation.

claim: The barn owl's frequency tuning is driven by ITD reliability rather than solely spatial tuning.
source: These results further support the hypothesis that the barn owl's frequency tuning is driven by ITD reliability rather than solely spatial tuning.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from the various control analyses.

claim: The majority of the barn owl's basilar papilla responds to 5–10 kHz.
source: The majority of the barn owl's basilar papilla responds to 5–10 kHz (Köppl et al., 1993), which may induce a bias toward high frequencies into the downstream auditory centers.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Köppl et al., 1993.

claim: The eardrum may have detection biases for frequencies above 3 kHz.
source: The eardrum itself may also have detection biases for frequencies above 3 kHz (Kettler et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kettler et al., 2016.

claim: The ICCls and midbrain maps contain few neurons tuned to frequencies below 1 kHz.
source: Consistently, the ICCls and midbrain maps contain few neurons tuned to frequencies below 1 kHz (Figure 4, Wagner et al., 2007; Cazettes et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 4 and citations to previous work.

claim: The cochlear and eardrum properties likely evolved simultaneously with the evolution of the facial ruff to facilitate the use of ITD detection at high frequencies.
source: While these properties are not expected to be affected by the facial ruff, they likely evolved simultaneously with the evolution of the facial ruff to facilitate the use of ITD detection at high frequencies.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about evolutionary relationships.

claim: The ICx mostly covers 30° ipsilateral to 90° contralateral space, which equates to approximately +90 µs to –300 µs ITD.
source: The ICx, as well as the downstream optic tectum, mostly cover 30° ipsilateral to 90° contralateral space, which equates to approximately +90 µs to –300 µs ITD (Knudsen, 1982; Knudsen, 1984; Cazettes et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The most rearward locations are significantly underrepresented in the auditory midbrain.
source: This means that the most rearward locations are significantly underrepresented in the auditory midbrain.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial coverage of the ICx.

claim: The changes in frequency tuning occurred in animals maintained in regular group aviaries with daily feeding and absence of specific task training or survival needs.
source: The changes in frequency tuning we found occurred in animals maintained in regular group aviaries with daily feeding and absence of specific task training or survival needs such as hunting experience or auditory-driven tasks.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental conditions.

claim: The shaping of the owl's ICx frequency tuning based on anticipated ITD reliability may be a normal and robust step in owl's development.
source: Thus, the shaping of the owl's ICx frequency tuning based on anticipated ITD reliability may be a normal and robust step in owl's development.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that changes occur without specific training.

claim: This work provides evidence that the brain can assess the reliability of an auditory spatial cue along normal development and experience-dependent changes.
source: In sum, this work provides evidence that the brain can assess the reliability of an auditory spatial cue along normal development and experience-dependent changes and use this information to drive neural tunings matching anticipated reliability across frequency and locations.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: This is the first description of the natural learning of cue reliability implemented in a midbrain network.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first description of the natural learning of cue reliability, where the learning is implemented in a midbrain network, in contrast with previous work finding similar results in the forebrain (Keating et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Anticipated ITD cue reliability has been shown to drive spatial discriminability in humans.
source: As anticipated ITD cue reliability has also been shown to drive spatial discriminability in humans (Pavão et al., 2020), it is possible that a similar learning process could occur as the human head and ears grow and develop.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pavão et al., 2020.
